title: Injuria sine damno and damnum sine injuria

content.overview: Injuria sine damno (violation of a legal right without proven actual loss) is actionable. Damnum sine injuria (actual loss without violation of a legal right) is not. These maxims frame whether the claimant has a cause of action at all.

sections.heading: Injuria sine damno
sections.body: Where a legal right is invaded, the law presumes damage. Classic illustrations: Ashby v. White (wrongful denial of vote); Bhim Singh v. State of J&K (illegal detention — compensation for rights violation). The point is rights-protection, not a balance-sheet of financial loss.

sections.heading: Damnum sine injuria
sections.body: Competition or lawful exercise of rights may cause loss without creating a tort. Gloucester Grammar School and Mogul Steamship illustrate loss from lawful rivalry. The claimant must show an invaded legal right, not only economic harm.

sections.heading: Application method
sections.body: Identify the precise legal right claimed. If none, dismiss on damnum sine injuria. If a right exists, liability may follow even without special damage unless the tort requires proof of damage.

hypotheticals.question: A shopkeeper lawfully undercuts prices; a rival loses customers. Actionable?
hypotheticals.analysis: Absent unlawful means, conspiracy of a prohibited kind, or infringement of a legal right, this is damnum sine injuria. Lawful competition is not a tort.

Confirmed para 63 (p. 110): express affirmation of the foundational tort rule that injuria sine damno is actionable while damnum sine injuria is not (quoting Justice G.P. Singh, Law of Torts).
Confirmed para 66 (p. 111): right to institute a civil action under Section 9 CPC for invasion of legal rights without needing a separate empowering statute (Ganga Bai v. Vijay Kumar, 1974).

Common-law and constitutional framework check: injuria sine damno governs actionable per se torts (trespass, libel, false imprisonment) and constitutional damages for rights violation (Bhim Singh, 1985); damnum sine injuria governs lawful competition and damage resulting from exercise of legal rights without legal wrong.

distinctions.title: Injuria sine damno
distinctions.left: Injuria sine damno: legal right violated; actual loss need not be proved. Actionable per se (e.g. Ashby v. White).
distinctions.right: Actionable in tort; damages awarded to vindicate the invaded legal right.

rows.left: No proof of financial loss required

distinctions.title: Damnum sine injuria
distinctions.left: Damnum sine injuria: actual loss suffered; no legal right infringed. Not actionable in tort (e.g. Gloucester Grammar School).
distinctions.right: No remedy in tort; lawful exercise of rights or lawful competition does not constitute a legal wrong.

caseLaw.name: Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India
caseLaw.holding: Judgment dated 13/05/2016. In para 63, the Supreme Court expressly affirmed the foundational principle of the law of torts in India, quoting Justice G.P. Singh: 'The principles which form the foundation of the law of torts are usually expressed by saying the injuria sine damno is actionable but damnum sine (or absque) injuria is not.' The Court confirmed that a civil suit under Section 9 CPC lies for the invasion of any legal right as a common-law remedy, whereas damnum without injuria confers no cause of action.
caseLaw.relevance: Direct authority for the foundational injuria sine damno / damnum sine injuria distinction in Indian tort law.
